note: Typical adult reference ranges for education. Laboratories differ — always use the range printed on your own report and discuss results with a doctor.

markers.name: Haemoglobin
markers.purpose: The iron-rich protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to every tissue.
markers.low: Anaemia — commonly from iron deficiency, low vitamin B12 or folate, blood loss (including heavy periods), chronic kidney disease or long-term illness. Can cause tiredness, breathlessness and pale skin.
markers.high: Dehydration, smoking, living at high altitude, long-term lung or heart disease, or rarely a marrow condition (polycythaemia).

markers.name: Red blood cell count
markers.purpose: The number of red blood cells in a volume of blood.
markers.low: Anaemia, blood loss, nutritional deficiency or marrow suppression.
markers.high: Dehydration, lung disease, high altitude or polycythaemia. A high count with small cells can suggest thalassaemia trait.

markers.name: Haematocrit (PCV)
markers.purpose: The percentage of your blood volume made up of red cells.
markers.high: Dehydration or excess red cell production.

markers.name: Mean corpuscular volume
markers.purpose: The average size of your red blood cells — a clue to the cause of anaemia.
markers.low: Small cells (microcytic): usually iron deficiency or thalassaemia trait.
markers.high: Large cells (macrocytic): vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, an underactive thyroid or some medicines.

markers.name: Mean corpuscular haemoglobin
markers.purpose: The average amount of haemoglobin in each red cell.
markers.high: B12 or folate deficiency.

markers.name: Mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration
markers.purpose: How concentrated the haemoglobin is inside red cells.
markers.high: Hereditary spherocytosis or a sample artefact.

markers.name: Red cell distribution width
markers.purpose: How much your red cells vary in size.
markers.high: Mixed or developing deficiencies (iron, B12, folate), recent bleeding or transfusion.

markers.name: White blood cell count
markers.purpose: The total number of infection-fighting white cells.
markers.low: Some viral infections, autoimmune conditions, certain medicines or marrow problems. A low count raises infection risk.
markers.high: Infection, inflammation, stress, steroid medicines, smoking or, rarely, leukaemia.

markers.name: Neutrophils
markers.purpose: The most common white cell, the first responder to bacterial infection.
markers.low: Viral infections, some medicines (including chemotherapy), B12/folate deficiency or autoimmune disease.
markers.high: Bacterial infection, inflammation, stress, steroids or recent exercise.

markers.name: Lymphocytes
markers.purpose: White cells that make antibodies (B cells) and kill infected cells (T cells).
markers.low: Stress, steroids, some viral infections (including HIV) or immune deficiency.
markers.high: Viral infections such as flu or glandular fever, whooping cough, or rarely lymphoma or leukaemia.

markers.name: Monocytes
markers.purpose: White cells that become macrophages, which engulf germs and debris.
markers.high: Chronic infections (such as TB), recovery from infection, inflammatory disease.

markers.name: Eosinophils
markers.purpose: White cells involved in allergy and fighting parasites.
markers.high: Allergies, asthma, eczema, parasitic worm infections or some medicines.

markers.name: Basophils
markers.purpose: The rarest white cell, releasing histamine in allergic reactions.
markers.high: Allergic reactions or, rarely, marrow disorders.

markers.name: Absolute neutrophil count
markers.purpose: The actual number of neutrophils — more useful than the percentage for judging infection risk.
markers.low: Neutropenia: a higher risk of bacterial infection, especially below 1.0.
markers.high: Bacterial infection, inflammation or steroid treatment.

markers.name: Platelet count
markers.purpose: Tiny cell fragments that plug leaks and start blood clotting.
markers.low: Viral infections (dengue is a classic cause), immune thrombocytopenia, liver disease, an enlarged spleen or some medicines. Very low counts cause easy bruising and bleeding.
markers.high: Inflammation, infection, iron deficiency, after surgery or bleeding, or rarely a marrow disorder.

markers.name: Mean platelet volume
markers.purpose: The average size of platelets; young platelets are larger.
markers.high: Platelets being used up and replaced quickly.

markers.name: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
markers.purpose: How fast red cells settle in a tube — a non-specific sign of inflammation.
markers.high: Infection, inflammatory or autoimmune disease (such as rheumatoid arthritis), anaemia, pregnancy or older age. It points to inflammation somewhere but not where.

markers.name: Reticulocyte count
markers.purpose: Young red cells — shows how actively the marrow is making new ones.
markers.low: The marrow isn't keeping up (deficiency or marrow problem).
markers.high: The marrow is responding to blood loss or red-cell breakdown.

markers.name: Bilirubin (total)
markers.purpose: A yellow pigment made when old red cells are broken down, processed by the liver and cleared in bile.
markers.high: Liver inflammation, blocked bile ducts (gallstones), faster red-cell breakdown or harmless Gilbert's syndrome. High levels cause jaundice.

markers.name: Bilirubin (direct)
markers.purpose: The conjugated bilirubin the liver has already processed.
markers.high: The liver can't pass bilirubin into bile — liver disease or a blocked bile duct.

markers.name: Bilirubin (indirect)
markers.purpose: Unconjugated bilirubin on its way to the liver.
markers.high: Red cells breaking down faster than usual, or Gilbert's syndrome.

markers.name: ALT (SGPT)
markers.purpose: An enzyme found mainly inside liver cells; it leaks into the blood when they are damaged.
markers.high: Liver cell injury — fatty liver, viral hepatitis, alcohol, some medicines or supplements. Mild rises are common and often temporary.

markers.name: AST (SGOT)
markers.purpose: An enzyme found in the liver, heart and muscles.
markers.high: Liver injury, muscle damage (including hard exercise) or heart muscle injury. An AST higher than ALT can point to alcohol-related liver disease.

markers.name: Alkaline phosphatase
markers.purpose: An enzyme from the bile ducts and bone.
markers.low: Rarely: zinc or magnesium deficiency, hypothyroidism.
markers.high: Blocked bile flow, or high bone turnover (growth in teenagers, healing fractures, vitamin D deficiency, bone disease). Normal in pregnancy.

markers.name: Gamma-glutamyl transferase
markers.purpose: A liver and bile-duct enzyme that is sensitive to alcohol.
markers.high: Alcohol use, fatty liver, blocked bile ducts or certain medicines. A high GGT with a high ALP points to the bile ducts rather than bone.

markers.name: Total protein
markers.purpose: All the proteins in blood plasma — mainly albumin and globulins.
markers.low: Liver disease, protein loss through the kidneys or gut, or malnutrition.
markers.high: Dehydration or chronic inflammation; rarely myeloma.

markers.name: Albumin
markers.purpose: The main protein made by the liver; it keeps fluid inside blood vessels and carries hormones and drugs.
markers.low: Liver disease, kidney protein loss (nephrotic syndrome), malnutrition or inflammation. Low albumin can cause swollen ankles.
markers.high: Usually dehydration.

markers.name: Globulin
markers.purpose: Proteins including antibodies and transport proteins.
markers.high: Chronic infection or inflammation, autoimmune disease or, rarely, myeloma.

markers.name: Albumin/globulin ratio
markers.purpose: The balance between albumin and globulins.
markers.low: Liver disease, kidney protein loss or high antibody levels.
markers.high: Usually not significant.

markers.name: Lactate dehydrogenase
markers.purpose: An enzyme in almost every tissue — raised whenever cells are damaged.
markers.high: Tissue damage anywhere: red-cell breakdown, liver, muscle, heart or lung injury.

markers.name: Ammonia
markers.purpose: A waste product of protein breakdown that the liver turns into urea.
markers.high: Severe liver disease, where it can affect the brain (hepatic encephalopathy).

markers.name: Creatinine
markers.purpose: A waste product from muscle that the kidneys filter out. The best single blood test of kidney filtering.
markers.low: Low muscle mass or pregnancy — usually not a concern.
markers.high: Reduced kidney function (acute or chronic), dehydration, very high muscle mass, high-protein diets or some medicines.

markers.name: Urea
markers.purpose: A waste product made by the liver from protein and cleared by the kidneys.
markers.low: Low protein intake, liver disease or pregnancy.
markers.high: Dehydration, reduced kidney function, a high-protein diet or bleeding in the stomach.

markers.name: Blood urea nitrogen
markers.purpose: The nitrogen part of urea; the US equivalent of the urea test.
markers.low: Low protein intake or liver disease.
markers.high: Dehydration or reduced kidney function.

markers.name: Uric acid
markers.purpose: A waste product from the breakdown of purines in food and cells.
markers.high: Gout (painful crystal arthritis, often in the big toe), kidney stones, kidney disease, alcohol, a purine-rich diet or some diuretics.

markers.name: eGFR
markers.purpose: Estimated glomerular filtration rate: how much blood your kidneys filter per minute, calculated from creatinine, age and sex.
markers.low: Reduced kidney function: 60–89 mildly reduced, 30–59 moderate chronic kidney disease, below 15 kidney failure. One low result should be repeated.
markers.high: Normal.

markers.name: Sodium
markers.purpose: The main salt in body fluid; it controls water balance and nerve and muscle function.
markers.low: Hyponatraemia: too much water relative to salt — some diuretics, heart, liver or kidney failure, heavy sweating, vomiting or excess ADH. Can cause confusion.
markers.high: Dehydration, not drinking enough, or rarely diabetes insipidus.

markers.name: Potassium
markers.purpose: A salt essential for heart rhythm and muscle function.
markers.low: Vomiting, diarrhoea or diuretics. Can cause muscle weakness and heart rhythm problems.
markers.high: Kidney disease, some blood-pressure medicines or a haemolysed (damaged) sample. Very high levels are dangerous for the heart.

markers.name: Chloride
markers.purpose: A salt that works with sodium to keep fluid and acid–base balance.
markers.high: Dehydration or some kidney and acid–base disorders.

markers.name: Bicarbonate
markers.purpose: The main buffer that keeps blood acidity in range.
markers.low: Metabolic acidosis — kidney disease, uncontrolled diabetes (ketoacidosis) or severe diarrhoea.
markers.high: Vomiting, diuretics or long-term lung disease.

markers.name: Calcium
markers.purpose: The mineral that builds bones and teeth and lets nerves, muscles and the heart work.
markers.low: Vitamin D deficiency, low parathyroid hormone, kidney disease or low albumin. Can cause tingling and cramps.
markers.high: Overactive parathyroid glands, too much vitamin D or calcium supplements, or some cancers.

markers.name: Ionised calcium
markers.purpose: The free, active form of calcium in the blood.
markers.low: Low parathyroid activity or vitamin D deficiency.
markers.high: Overactive parathyroid glands.

markers.name: Phosphorus
markers.purpose: A mineral that pairs with calcium in bone and powers cell energy.
markers.high: Kidney disease or underactive parathyroid.

markers.name: Magnesium
markers.purpose: A mineral needed for muscles, nerves, heart rhythm and hundreds of enzymes.
markers.low: Poor diet, alcohol, diarrhoea or diuretics; can cause cramps and palpitations.
markers.high: Kidney disease or supplements/antacids.

markers.name: Total cholesterol
markers.purpose: All the cholesterol in your blood — a building block for cells and hormones that can also clog arteries.
markers.high: A higher risk of fatty deposits in the arteries (atherosclerosis), heart attack and stroke — interpret together with LDL and HDL.

markers.name: LDL cholesterol
markers.purpose: 'Bad' cholesterol: the particles that deposit cholesterol in artery walls.
markers.high: The main target for preventing heart attacks and strokes. Diet, exercise, weight and sometimes statin medicines lower it.

markers.name: HDL cholesterol
markers.purpose: 'Good' cholesterol: it carries cholesterol away from arteries back to the liver.
markers.low: A higher heart risk. Exercise, stopping smoking and losing weight raise HDL.
markers.high: Generally protective.

markers.name: Triglycerides
markers.purpose: Fats carried in the blood from food and made by the liver from excess sugar and alcohol.
markers.high: Higher heart risk, often with excess weight, sugar, alcohol or diabetes. Very high levels (above 500–1000) can inflame the pancreas.

markers.name: VLDL cholesterol
markers.purpose: Very-low-density lipoprotein, which mainly carries triglycerides.
markers.high: Usually goes with high triglycerides.

markers.name: Non-HDL cholesterol
markers.purpose: Total cholesterol minus HDL — all the artery-clogging particles together.
markers.high: Higher cardiovascular risk.

markers.name: Cholesterol/HDL ratio
markers.purpose: A risk ratio: lower is better (ideally under 3.5).
markers.high: Higher cardiovascular risk.

markers.name: LDL/HDL ratio
markers.purpose: Another risk ratio; lower is better.
markers.high: Higher cardiovascular risk.

markers.name: Lipoprotein(a)
markers.purpose: A mostly inherited cholesterol particle that raises heart risk independently of LDL.
markers.high: An inherited extra risk factor for heart disease and stroke.

markers.name: Fasting glucose
markers.purpose: Blood sugar after at least 8 hours without food.
markers.low: Hypoglycaemia — too much diabetes medicine, missed meals, alcohol or rarely a hormone problem. Causes shakiness, sweating and confusion.
markers.high: 100–125 suggests prediabetes and 126 or more on two occasions suggests diabetes.

markers.name: Post-meal glucose (2 h)
markers.purpose: Blood sugar two hours after a meal or glucose drink.
markers.high: 140–199 suggests prediabetes and 200 or more suggests diabetes.

markers.name: Random glucose
markers.purpose: Blood sugar at any time of day.
markers.high: Above 200 with symptoms suggests diabetes; otherwise repeat as a fasting test or HbA1c.

markers.name: HbA1c
markers.purpose: Glycated haemoglobin: the average blood sugar over the past 2–3 months.
markers.low: Rarely significant; can be falsely low with anaemia or recent blood loss.
markers.high: 5.7–6.4% is the prediabetes range and 6.5% or above the diabetes range. In diabetes, lower HbA1c protects the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart.

markers.name: Fasting insulin
markers.purpose: The hormone that moves sugar into cells.
markers.low: Type 1 diabetes or advanced type 2 diabetes.
markers.high: Insulin resistance — common with excess weight, PCOS and prediabetes.

markers.name: C-peptide
markers.purpose: Released with insulin in equal amounts — shows how much insulin the pancreas itself is making.
markers.low: The pancreas makes little insulin (type 1 diabetes).
markers.high: Insulin resistance or kidney disease.

markers.name: TSH
markers.purpose: Thyroid-stimulating hormone from the pituitary. It rises when the thyroid is underactive and falls when it is overactive.
markers.low: An overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism, e.g. Graves' disease), too much thyroxine medicine, or rarely a pituitary problem.
markers.high: An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism, often Hashimoto's). Causes tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold and constipation.

markers.name: Total T3
markers.purpose: Triiodothyronine, the most active thyroid hormone.
markers.high: Overactive thyroid.

markers.name: Total T4
markers.purpose: Thyroxine, the main hormone released by the thyroid.
markers.high: Overactive thyroid, or high binding proteins (pregnancy, the pill).

markers.name: Free T3
markers.purpose: The unbound, active part of T3.
markers.high: Overactive thyroid.

markers.name: Free T4
markers.purpose: The unbound, active part of T4 — the best measure of thyroid output.
markers.high: Overactive thyroid or too much thyroxine medicine.

markers.name: Anti-TPO antibodies
markers.purpose: Antibodies against the thyroid's own enzyme.
markers.high: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's or Graves'), which may affect thyroid function now or later.

markers.name: Vitamin D (25-OH)
markers.purpose: The storage form of vitamin D, made in the skin in sunlight and activated by the liver and kidneys. It controls calcium absorption and bone strength.
markers.low: Very common, especially with little sun exposure or darker skin. Can cause weak, aching bones and muscle weakness; 20–29 is insufficient and under 20 deficient.
markers.high: Usually from high-dose supplements; above 100–150 risks high calcium.

markers.name: Vitamin B12
markers.purpose: A vitamin needed to make red cells and keep nerves healthy. Absorbing it needs intrinsic factor from the stomach and a healthy ileum.
markers.low: Vegetarian or vegan diets, pernicious anaemia, stomach or gut disease, or long-term metformin or acid-reducing medicines. Causes anaemia with large red cells and numbness or tingling.
markers.high: Usually supplements; occasionally liver disease.

markers.name: Folate
markers.purpose: Folic acid (vitamin B9), needed for making DNA and red cells and vital in early pregnancy.
markers.low: Poor diet, alcohol, gut disease or some medicines; causes anaemia with large red cells.
markers.high: Usually supplements.

markers.name: Serum iron
markers.purpose: The iron circulating in the blood, bound to transferrin. It swings a lot through the day.
markers.high: Iron overload (haemochromatosis), supplements or liver damage.

markers.name: Ferritin
markers.purpose: The body's iron store. The earliest and most reliable sign of iron deficiency.
markers.low: Iron deficiency, even before anaemia develops — usually from diet, heavy periods or blood loss from the gut.
markers.high: Inflammation or infection (ferritin rises with inflammation), liver disease, alcohol or iron overload.

markers.name: Total iron-binding capacity
markers.purpose: How much iron the blood's transport protein could carry. It rises when iron stores are low.
markers.high: Iron deficiency or pregnancy.

markers.name: Transferrin saturation
markers.purpose: The percentage of transferrin that is carrying iron.
markers.high: Iron overload (haemochromatosis).

markers.name: Zinc
markers.purpose: A trace mineral for immunity, wound healing, taste and growth.
markers.low: Poor diet, gut disease or alcohol.
markers.high: Excess supplements.

markers.name: Troponin I
markers.purpose: A protein released only when heart muscle cells are damaged.
markers.high: Heart muscle injury — most importantly a heart attack. A raised troponin with chest pain needs emergency care.

markers.name: Troponin T
markers.purpose: A heart-muscle protein used to detect heart attacks.
markers.high: Heart muscle injury; also mildly raised in kidney disease.

markers.name: CK-MB
markers.purpose: The heart form of creatine kinase, an older marker of heart damage.
markers.high: Heart muscle injury (troponin is now preferred).

markers.name: Creatine kinase
markers.purpose: An enzyme that leaks from damaged muscle.
markers.high: Muscle injury or very hard exercise, statin side effects, muscle disease, or heart damage.

markers.name: BNP
markers.purpose: B-type natriuretic peptide, released when the heart's ventricles are stretched.
markers.high: Heart failure — the higher, the more strain on the heart. Also rises with kidney disease and age.

markers.name: NT-proBNP
markers.purpose: A fragment released with BNP — a sensitive test for heart strain.
markers.high: Heart failure or strain; cut-offs rise with age.

markers.name: hs-CRP
markers.purpose: A high-sensitivity test for low-grade inflammation, used to refine heart risk.
markers.high: 1–3 average and above 3 higher cardiovascular risk — if there's no infection at the time.

markers.name: C-reactive protein
markers.purpose: A protein the liver makes quickly in response to inflammation or infection.
markers.high: Infection (especially bacterial), injury or inflammatory disease. Very high values usually mean significant infection.

markers.name: Homocysteine
markers.purpose: An amino acid that builds up when B12, folate or B6 are low.
markers.high: B12 or folate deficiency, kidney disease or inherited conditions; linked to artery disease and clots.

markers.name: Amylase
markers.purpose: A starch-digesting enzyme from the pancreas and salivary glands.
markers.high: Acute pancreatitis, blocked pancreatic duct, or salivary gland problems such as mumps.

markers.name: Lipase
markers.purpose: A fat-digesting enzyme made almost only by the pancreas.
markers.high: Acute pancreatitis (usually over 3× the upper limit), gallstones or pancreatic duct blockage.

markers.name: Cortisol (morning)
markers.purpose: The main stress hormone, made by the adrenal glands; highest in the morning.
markers.low: Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) or pituitary problems — tiredness, low blood pressure.
markers.high: Stress, steroid medicines or Cushing's syndrome.

markers.name: Testosterone (total)
markers.purpose: The main male sex hormone, also present in smaller amounts in women.
markers.low: In men: low energy, libido and muscle mass (hypogonadism).
markers.high: In women: polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) or adrenal causes; in men, supplements.

markers.name: Oestradiol (E2)
markers.purpose: The main oestrogen; in women it varies widely across the menstrual cycle.
markers.low: Menopause, low ovarian function or low body weight.
markers.high: Ovulation, pregnancy, some medicines or ovarian cysts.

markers.name: Progesterone
markers.purpose: A hormone from the ovary after ovulation that prepares the womb for pregnancy.
markers.low: No ovulation in that cycle, or early pregnancy problems.
markers.high: Ovulation has happened, or pregnancy.

markers.name: Luteinising hormone
markers.purpose: A pituitary hormone that triggers ovulation and testosterone production.
markers.high: Menopause, PCOS or failing testes/ovaries; peaks at ovulation.

markers.name: Follicle-stimulating hormone
markers.purpose: A pituitary hormone that grows egg follicles and supports sperm production.
markers.high: Menopause or reduced ovarian/testicular function.

markers.name: Prolactin
markers.purpose: The pituitary hormone that makes milk.
markers.high: Pregnancy and breastfeeding, stress, some medicines, an underactive thyroid or a pituitary tumour (prolactinoma).

markers.name: PSA (total)
markers.purpose: Prostate-specific antigen, a protein made by the prostate.
markers.high: Prostate enlargement, infection or inflammation, recent ejaculation or cycling — and sometimes prostate cancer. Needs a doctor's interpretation.

markers.name: Anti-Müllerian hormone
markers.purpose: A hormone from small ovarian follicles — an estimate of egg reserve.
markers.low: Lower ovarian reserve (falls naturally with age).
markers.high: Polycystic ovary syndrome.

markers.name: Beta hCG
markers.purpose: The pregnancy hormone made by the placenta.
markers.high: Pregnancy — or rarely certain tumours.

markers.name: DHEA-S
markers.purpose: An adrenal androgen that declines with age.
markers.high: PCOS or adrenal overactivity.

markers.name: Parathyroid hormone
markers.purpose: The hormone that raises blood calcium by drawing on bone and saving calcium in the kidneys.
markers.low: Underactive parathyroid glands (often after neck surgery).
markers.high: Overactive parathyroid glands, or a response to low vitamin D or kidney disease.

markers.name: ACTH
markers.purpose: The pituitary hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol.
markers.high: Addison's disease or Cushing's disease.

markers.name: Urine pH
markers.purpose: How acidic or alkaline the urine is.
markers.low: Acidic urine: high-protein diets, uncontrolled diabetes, dehydration.
markers.high: Alkaline urine: vegetarian diets, some infections, kidney stones of certain types.

markers.name: Urine specific gravity
markers.purpose: How concentrated the urine is.
markers.low: Very dilute urine: drinking a lot, diuretics or kidneys that can't concentrate.
markers.high: Concentrated urine: dehydration.

markers.name: Urine protein
markers.purpose: Protein in urine. Healthy kidneys keep protein in the blood.
markers.high: Kidney filter damage (from diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney disease), fever, hard exercise or infection.

markers.name: Urine glucose
markers.purpose: Sugar in urine; it spills over when blood sugar is high.
markers.high: High blood sugar (diabetes), pregnancy or some diabetes medicines (SGLT2 inhibitors).

markers.name: Urine ketones
markers.purpose: Ketones appear when the body burns fat for fuel.
markers.high: Fasting, low-carb diets, vomiting — or dangerous diabetic ketoacidosis in people with diabetes.

markers.name: Urine blood
markers.purpose: Blood or haemoglobin in the urine, often invisible to the eye.
markers.high: Infection, kidney stones, periods, hard exercise, kidney disease or, less often, bladder or kidney tumours.

markers.name: Urine bilirubin
markers.purpose: Bilirubin in urine — normally absent.
markers.high: Liver disease or blocked bile ducts (urine looks dark).

markers.name: Urine nitrite
markers.purpose: Made by many bacteria from nitrates in urine.
markers.high: A bacterial urinary tract infection is likely.

markers.name: Urine pus cells
markers.purpose: White blood cells in the urine.
markers.high: Urinary tract infection or inflammation (a few more is normal in women).

markers.name: Urine red cells
markers.purpose: Red blood cells seen under the microscope.
markers.high: Infection, stones, exercise, periods or kidney disease.

markers.name: Urine epithelial cells
markers.purpose: Cells shed from the lining of the urinary tract.
markers.high: Usually a contaminated sample; sometimes inflammation.

markers.name: Urine microalbumin
markers.purpose: Tiny amounts of albumin in urine — the earliest sign of kidney damage from diabetes or high blood pressure.
markers.high: Early kidney damage; controlling blood sugar and pressure can reverse it.

markers.name: Albumin/creatinine ratio
markers.purpose: Urine albumin corrected for concentration — the standard kidney-damage screen.
markers.high: 30–300 moderately and above 300 severely increased albuminuria.

markers.name: Prothrombin time
markers.purpose: How long blood takes to clot through the 'extrinsic' pathway, which depends on liver-made clotting factors and vitamin K.
markers.high: Warfarin, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency or clotting factor problems.

markers.name: INR
markers.purpose: A standardised version of the prothrombin time. People on warfarin are usually aimed at 2–3.
markers.high: Warfarin (expected), liver disease or vitamin K deficiency.

markers.name: aPTT
markers.purpose: Clotting time through the 'intrinsic' pathway.
markers.high: Heparin, haemophilia, von Willebrand disease or lupus anticoagulant.

markers.name: D-dimer
markers.purpose: A fragment released when a blood clot breaks down.
markers.low: Normal — helps rule out a clot.
markers.high: Possible clot (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism), but also infection, pregnancy, surgery and older age.

markers.name: Fibrinogen
markers.purpose: The liver-made protein that forms the mesh of a clot.
markers.low: Liver disease or clotting being used up (DIC).
markers.high: Inflammation, pregnancy or smoking.

markers.name: Hepatitis B surface antigen
markers.purpose: A protein from the hepatitis B virus.
markers.high: Current hepatitis B infection. Needs follow-up with a doctor.

markers.name: Hepatitis C antibody
markers.purpose: Antibodies to the hepatitis C virus.
markers.high: Past or current hepatitis C; a follow-up viral load test tells which.

markers.name: Rheumatoid factor
markers.purpose: An antibody often present in rheumatoid arthritis.
markers.high: Rheumatoid arthritis, other autoimmune diseases, chronic infection — or healthy older people.

markers.name: Anti-CCP antibodies
markers.purpose: A very specific antibody test for rheumatoid arthritis.
markers.high: Rheumatoid arthritis is likely, sometimes years before symptoms.

markers.name: ASO titre
markers.purpose: Antibodies after a streptococcal throat infection.
markers.high: A recent strep infection; relevant to rheumatic fever, which can damage heart valves.

markers.name: Procalcitonin
markers.purpose: A marker that rises sharply in bacterial infection.
markers.high: Significant bacterial infection or sepsis.

markers.name: CEA
markers.purpose: Carcinoembryonic antigen, used to monitor some cancers (especially bowel).
markers.high: Smoking, inflammation and some cancers. Not a screening test on its own.

markers.name: CA-125
markers.purpose: A protein used to monitor ovarian cancer treatment.
markers.high: Periods, endometriosis, fibroids, pregnancy — and ovarian cancer. Not a screening test on its own.

markers.name: CA 19-9
markers.purpose: A marker used to monitor pancreatic and bile-duct cancers.
markers.high: Bile-duct blockage, pancreatitis — and some cancers.

markers.name: Alpha-fetoprotein
markers.purpose: A protein made by the fetal liver; in adults it is used to monitor some liver and testicular tumours.
markers.high: Pregnancy, liver disease — or liver or testicular tumours.
